text: products of vectors. A vector can be multiplied by another vector, but may not be divided by a vector. There are two kinds of vector products, scalar multiplication, dot product, or vector multiplication, cross product. As the names imply, the result of the multiplication produces either a scalar or a vector. The dot product. The scalar product of two vectors is denoted using the dot symbol, written in latex source as backslash cdot. Instead of the normal time symbol, written in latex source as backslash times. The scalar product of vectors vector a and vector b is defined by vector a dot vector b equals a b cos phi, where the angle phi represents an angle between the two vectors. Note, in latex there are two versions of phi. The source command backslash var phi and the source command backslash phi both mean the same thing, but you need to be consistent. In the definition of the dot product, the direction of the angle phi does not matter due to the property of cos phi equals cos of negative phi. That is, cosine is an even function. The dot product is a negative number in quadrant two, because cosine of phi is less than zero when pi over two is less than phi and phi is less than pi. And cosine of phi is greater than zero when zero is less than phi and phi is less than pi over two. When two vectors are parallel, the angle phi equals zero and vector a dot vector b equals a b cos zero equals a b. What happens when the vectors are anti-parallel or perpendicular? For anti-parallel vectors, vector a dot vector b equals negative a b. For perpendicular or orthogonal vectors, vector a dot vector b equals zero. The scalar product of a vector with itself is the square of its magnitude. Vector a to the power of two, equivalent vector a dot vector a equals a a cos of zero equals a squared. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. The dot product of two vectors is negative. Is the angle between the vectors less than equal to or greater than 90 degrees? Rules using unit vectors. In the Cartesian coordinate system, scalar products of a unit vector with another different unit vector vanish because these unit vectors are orthogonal. i hat dot j hat equals cos of pi over two equals zero. i hat dot k hat equals cos of pi over two equals zero. k hat dot j hat equals cos of pi over two equals zero. We often take advantage of the fact that the magnitudes of all unit vectors are one. The magnitude of i hat equals i hat dot i hat equals i squared equals one. The magnitude of j hat equals j hat dot j hat equals j squared equals one. The magnitude of k hat equals k hat dot k hat equals k squared equals one. The scalar product is also interpreted as the projection of one vector onto the direction of the other vector, i.e. projection A sub parallel onto the direction of vector B. Vector A dot vector B equals A B cos phi equals B times A cos phi equals B A parallel equals A times B cos phi equals A B parallel. Recall the definitions of the vector components A sub X and A sub Y. We can define these quantities through the dot product with the appropriate unit vector. For example, using the vector A equals A sub X i hat plus A sub Y j hat, vector A dot i hat equals A sub X times i hat dot i hat plus A sub Y times i hat dot j hat equals A sub X cos of 0 plus A sub Y cos of pi over 2 equals A sub X. Vector A dot j hat equals A sub X times j hat dot i hat plus A sub Y times j hat dot j hat equals A sub X cos of pi over 2 plus A sub Y cos of 0 equals A sub Y. Scalar multiplication follows the previous properties of vector operation where they are commutative vector A dot vector B equals vector B dot vector A. Distributive vector A dot vector B plus vector C equals vector A dot vector B plus vector A dot vector C. We can compute the scalar products of two vectors using the distributive property. Vector A dot vector B equals A sub X i hat plus A sub Y j hat plus A sub Z k hat dot B sub X i hat plus B sub Y j hat plus B sub Z k hat equals A sub X B sub X i hat dot i hat plus A sub X B sub Y i hat dot j hat plus A sub X B sub Z i hat dot k hat plus A sub Y B sub X j hat dot i hat plus A sub Y B sub Y j hat dot j hat plus A sub Y B sub Z j hat dot K hat plus a sub z b sub x k hat dot i hat plus a sub z b sub y k hat dot j hat plus a sub z b sub z k hat dot k hat. Applying our rules for the dot products of unit vectors, the above expression simplifies quickly to vector a dot vector b equals a sub x b sub x plus a sub y b sub y plus a sub z b sub z. If we know the magnitudes a and b and the vector components of each vector, then we can solve for the angle phi between them. Cos phi equals vector a dot vector b over a b equals a sub x b sub x plus a sub y b sub y plus a sub z b sub z over a b. phi equals coast to the power of 1 a sub x b sub x plus a sub y b sub y plus a sub z b sub z over a b. Example problem, angle between two forces. The problem, three dogs are pulling on a stick in different directions. The first dog pulls with force vector f1 equals 10.0 i hat minus 20.4 j hat plus 2.0 k hat newtons. The second dog pulls with force vector f2 equals minus 15.0 i hat minus 6.2 k hat newtons. And the third dog pulls with force vector f3 equals 5.0 i hat plus 12.5 j hat newtons. What is the angle between the forces vector f1 and vector f2? The figure is shown on the course web page. The worked solution follows. The model. We treat each pull on the stick as a three-dimensional force vector expressed in Cartesian component form. The coordinate axes are arbitrary but fixed. The i hat, j hat and k hat directions are mutually perpendicular and form a right-handed coordinate system. The angle between two vectors is determined entirely by their components and magnitudes. We therefore model the angle between vector f1 and vector f2 using the scalar dot product which relates the cosine of the angle between two vectors to their components. The math. The angle between two vectors can be found from the scalar product. For the forces vector f1 and vector f2, the scalar product is related to the angle phi by vector f1 dot vector f2 equals f1 f2 cos phi. The magnitudes of the two forces are determined from their rectangular components. f1 equals the square root of 10.0 squared plus negative 20.4 squared plus 2.0 squared equals 22.8 newtons. f2 equals the square root of negative 15 squared plus 0.0 squared plus negative 6.2 squared equals 16.2 newtons. The scalar product is found by multiplying matching components and adding the products. Vector f1 dot vector f2 equals f sub 1x f sub 2x plus f sub 1y f sub 2y plus f sub 1z f sub 2z equals 10.0 times negative 15.0 plus negative 20.4 times 0 plus 2.0 times negative 6.2. equals negative 162.4 newtons to the power of 2. Solving the scalar product relation for cos phi gives cos phi equals f1 dot f2 over f1 f2 equals negative 162.4 over 22.8 times 16.2. equals negative 0.439. The angle between the two forces is obtained by taking the inverse cosine. phi equals cos to the power of negative 1 of negative 0.439 equals 116.0 degrees. The conclusion. The angle between the forces vector f1 and vector f2 is phi equals 116.0 degrees. Because the scalar product is negative, the angle between the two forces is greater than 90 degrees indicating that the dogs are pulling in substantially opposing directions. The cross product. The vector product yields, you guessed it, a vector. The vector product of two vectors is denoted by vector a cross vector b and is often called the cross product due to the times operator written in latex source as backslash times. The vector product produces a vector that is perpendicular to the plane containing both vectors. The magnitude of the vector product is defined as absolute value of vector a cross vector b equals a b sine phi, where phi represents the angle measured between the two vectors. In this case, the direction or sine of phi makes a difference because sine of negative phi equals negative sine phi. Sine is an odd function. In contrast to the scalar product, the vector product vanishes for pairs of vectors that are either parallel, where phi equals 0, or antiparallel, where phi equals pi, because sine of pi and sine of 0 both equals 0. The vector product and right-hand rule figures are shown on the course web page. The figure above shows that on the line perpendicular to the plane, there are two alternative directions. In the standard right-handed orientation, where phi is measured counterclockwise from the first vector, the resulting vector points upward. If we reverse phi, then the resulting vector points downward. This means the vector product is anti-communative because it reverses sine when the multiplication order is reversed. Vector a cross vector b equals negative vector b cross vector a. The right-hand rule helps determine the direction of the vector product. Use the index finger for vector a, the middle finger for vector b, and the thumb for the vector product vector a cross vector b on the right hand. Similar to the dot product, the cross product is distributive. Vector a cross open parentheses vector b plus vector c, closed parentheses equals open parentheses vector a cross vector b, closed parentheses plus open parentheses vector a cross vector c, closed parentheses. When we apply the definition of the cross product to the Cartesian unit vectors i hat j hat and k hat, we find that i hat cross i hat j hat cross j hat and k hat cross k hat all equals 0. What makes this so? All other cross products must have a magnitude equal to unity because the unit vectors are orthogonal. For example, absolute value of i hat cross j hat equals i j sine of pi over 2, which equals 1. The vector product must be along the z axis following negative k hat or positive k hat. Following the right-hand rule, we arrive at the relations i hat cross j hat equals positive k hat, j hat cross k hat equals positive i hat and k hat cross i hat equals positive j hat. The three unit vectors appear in a cyclic order to produce the next vector. The unit vector cube figure is shown on the course web page. We can use the distributive property and unit vector identities for the vector product. The full component derivation is shown on the course web page. The final component form is vector a cross vector b equals open parenthesis a sub y b sub z closed parenthesis i hat plus open parenthesis a sub z b sub x minus a sub x b sub z closed parenthesis j hat plus open parenthesis a sub x b sub y minus a sub y b sub x closed parenthesis k hat. The problem a wrench is used to loosen a rusty nut a force of 20.0 newtons is applied to the handle at a distance of 0.25 meters from the nut see the figure on the course web page. In a if the force is applied at an angle phi equals 40 degrees relative to the wrench handle what are the magnitude and direction of the torque applied to the nut b how do the magnitude and direction of the torque change if the force is instead applied at phi equals 45 degrees see for what value of phi does the torque have its maximum magnitude. The figure is shown on the course web page. The model we model the nut as a fixed pivot point and the wrench handle as a radial line extending away from that pivot point the applied force acts at a point on the wrench handle and makes an angle with the radial direction. The torque describes the turning effect of the force about the nut since the radial vector and the applied force lie in the plane of the wrench the torque vector must point perpendicular to that plane its direction is determined by the right hand rule and its magnitude depends on the lever arm the force magnitude and the angle between them. The math the magnitude of the torque produced by a force applied at an angle phi relative to the radial direction is tau equals RF sine phi for this wrench the lever arm is R equals 0.25 meters and the applied force has magnitude F equals 20.0 newtons. A when the force is applied at phi equals 40 degrees the torque magnitude is determined by inserting this angle into the torque expression tau equals 0.25 meters times 20.0 newtons times sine 40 degrees equals 3.21 newtons dot meter. The direction is determined from the right hand rule applied to vector R times vector F for the orientation shown in part A the torque points in the positive Z direction which is out of the page B when the force is applied at phi equals 45 degrees the same torque expression gives tau equals 0.25 meters times 20.0 newtons times sine 40.0 times sine. The right hand rule gives a torque in the negative Z direction which is into the page C the torque magnitude is largest when sine phi has its maximum value since the largest possible value of sine phi is 1 the maximum torque occurs when phi equals 90 degrees. The largest possible torque magnitude is therefore tau sub max equals RF equals 0.25 meters times 20.0 newtons equals 5.00 newtons dot meter. The conclusion for phi equals 40 degrees the torque has magnitude tau equals 3.21 newtons dot meter and points in the positive Z direction out of the page for phi equals 45 degrees the torque has magnitude tau equals 3.53 newtons dot meter and points in the negative Z direction into the page. The maximum possible torque occurs when phi equals 90 degrees giving tau sub max equals 5.00 newtons dot meter. The torque increases as the force becomes more perpendicular to the wrench tendle and its direction is set by the right hand rule.
